Book 20 of the Analects, 堯曰 Yáo yuē, named, as every book is, from its first words — "Yao said". The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 20 is the last and the shortest, three passages in all. The first is not a saying of the Master's at all but a string of words and deeds of the founding kings: Yao's charge to Shun as he hands on the throne (the order Heaven reckons out now rests in you; hold truly to the mean), given again by Shun to Yu; Tang's declaration to the High Lord on Heaven as he overthrows the Xia (the guilt of the people lies on me); and King Wu's gifts to good men, his words on humane men and kin, and his work of government — true weights and measures, lapsed offices filled, fallen states and broken lines restored (20.1). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: the book ends with these to show that what the sages' learning hands down is one and the same. In the second, Zizhang asks what fits a man to govern, and the Master names five excellences and four evils, which Zhu Xi, quoting Yin Tun, calls the most complete answer on government anywhere in the Analects (20.2). The third is the last saying of the Analects: without knowing the decree, the rites and words, one cannot be a gentleman, stand, or know men (20.3). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.
